key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court did not accept any key evidence, as it found the evidence regarding the last seen theory and Call Detail Records (CDRs) to be unreliable and lacking in confidence.
witness_credibility: The court found the witnesses' credibility to be questionable, noting inconsistencies in their statements and the unreliability of their testimonies, particularly regarding the identification parade and the CDRs.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 10th September 2009; Trial judgment: 17th May 2013; High Court decision: 5th August 2014; Supreme Court decision: August 2023

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Sanctity of test identification parade before the court is doubtful since the accused were already shown to the witnesses in the Police Station
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted and sentenced; High Court: Dismissed appeals; Supreme Court: Appeals allowed, judgment and order quashed and set aside
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused Prem Singh fled the scene of the incident and was apprehended two days later. They relied on the testimony of Jai Singh and Naresh Kumar, as well as the Call Detail Records (CDRs) to establish the guilt of the accused. The prosecution also claimed that the accused had a history of conflict with the deceased and that they committed the murder.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to establish the case beyond reasonable doubt. They emphasized the unreliability of the circumstantial evidence, particularly the last seen theory and the CDRs. The defence also highlighted the flaws in the identification process and the lack of conclusive evidence linking the accused to the crime.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that for a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established, consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt, and exclude every possible hypothesis except that the accused is guilty. The court emphasized that suspicion cannot replace proof beyond reasonable doubt.
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116 : [1985] 1 SCR 88
other_sentence_order: The appellants are acquitted of all charges. They are directed to be set at liberty if not required in any other case. Bail bonds of the appellants shall stand discharged. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
